Make chief of staff, that’s the only bot you talk to. Talk to the bot about your goal and have the chief suggest a team that could work towards your goal.

 If it’s fitness it might be a “Diet & Nutrition Bot”, a “strength training coach bot”, a “chef and recipes bot” etc.

If it’s business it might be a “books” (accounting), ops and estimating (pricing for projects), a marketing bot.

They have their own little desktop computers and you can even watch them work. They can set up and organize your calendar and update it based on your needs. It can call and negotiate your bills, fix credit etc with a wealth and clean slate bot. It will organize, read important emails and give you insights, reminders, and draft email replies based on your needs. It can make you a website or an image and can organize your Google Drive folders. 

If you’re ever stuck, just ask grok bot what the next best move is and it’ll provide a lot of clarity. You can even ask it how it can find a way to pay for itself lol

-go play around and ask it about its capabilities and talk to it about whatever goals are most important to you. It could plan vacations and find new restaurants or work on engineering designs.. much more besides business and health 👍🏻

I'd build a company that uses AI throughout its work in this order:

1. Build yourself a second brain. Keep markdown files in one folder explaining how you think, write and make decisions (obsidian).

2. Add voice notes throughout the day (wispr). Have an agent file every fact, story and decision where it belongs.

3. Build a brain for the company too. Include customers, calls, metrics, pricing, playbooks and past decisions, with the reasoning behind them.

4. Capture all your calls and meetings (granola). Send the transcripts directly into the company brain.

5. Keep a file of verified facts. Spell out what agents can truthfully say about you and the company so they don't invent claims.

6. Make a file for your writing voice. Include your best 50 posts, 20 you dislike and any words you avoid.

7. Version the whole thing with git (github). Every edit should have a history you can check.

8. Add one top-level instruction file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). Tell agents to read these files before working, avoid overwriting them and include dates.

9. Give agents memory that carries between sessions (claude-mem, mem0). They shouldn't have to start from nothing every time.

10. Bring all your data into a warehouse agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). Include advertising, analytics, CRM and payment data.

11. Give agents information other people don't have. Competitors can't download the context you've collected yourself.

the skills

12. Start by installing solid existing skills (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills). You don't need to begin with a blank slate.

13. Add marketing skills too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills).

14. List the company's workflows. Rank them by how much money they generate or save.

15. Record yourself walking through each workflow once. Say what you're doing as you go, including the steps you'd usually skip explaining.

16. Ask an agent to turn that recording into a skill. Include when to use it, the process, validation and common mistakes.

17. Keep each skill focused on one job. A small, plain skill is easier to use than a massive prompt.

18. Connect your tools through MCPs so agents can act on their suggestions (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase).

19. Give agents browser access (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome).

20. Set up a computer for agents to use when a tool has no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo).

21. Share your strongest skills publicly. A useful skill can be your next lead magnet.

the agents

22. Keep an orchestrator running continuously (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). Have it coordinate a dedicated agent for each project, with each project agent directing its own sub-agents.

23. Assign the build work to coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, cursor, t3, antigravity).

24. Put a harness around them for planning, testing and memory (ECC, superpowers).

25. Oversee the agents from one place (paperclip). Give each a role, spending limit and activity log you can inspect.

26. Trigger your skills automatically (n8n, scheduled tasks). Set daily and weekly runs, plus triggers for new leads and cancellations.

27. Route work to the right models (openrouter). Use the expensive one for planning and review (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), and cheaper ones for high-volume work.

28. Reduce token spending with concise responses and smaller tool outputs (caveman). Keep the output focused on what the next step needs.

29. Use a local model to keep sensitive data on your machine (gemma 4).

30. Measure what each job costs. Fix or remove any job that spends more than it brings in.

the factory

31. Set up the production line: specification agent → parallel building agents (git worktrees) → testing agent → reviewing agent → deployment (vercel, railway).

32. Send design through the same line (paper MCP). Include a skill that removes the parts that look AI-generated (unslop).

33. Turn each frustrating company task into an internal tool before the day ends.

34. Turn each customer request into a pull request before it reaches a human (tstack for the PR workflow).

35. Give reviewing agents an explicit quality bar: "is this something the world's best team would release?" Keep rejecting the work until it meets that standard.

36. Keep 50 real examples paired with correct answers. Rerun them whenever a new model arrives, then move to the model that performs best.

37. Keep approvals, accountability and customer conversations with humans. Those are the 10% you hold onto.

the loop

38. Send lessons from every completed job back into the brain. Record what worked, what failed and what to stop doing.

39. Bring in support tickets, analytics and social replies each night.

40. Have an agent update the playbooks every Friday using that week's outcomes. Review and approve its diff.

41. Once a month, rank everything by profit per human hour. Drop one activity and double down on another.

the growth

42. Have agents do the research before you spend any money (perplexity API, last30days skill).

43. Automate outbound from lead discovery through enrichment, verification and sending (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster).

44. Give prospects completed work they can use instead of a sales pitch.

45. Run advertising as a continuous loop. Have an agent create the ad, publish it through the facebook ads API, stop poor performers and expand the successful ones.

46. Have agents produce the creative assets too: images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs) and music (lyria 3.5, suno).

47. Make content from each completed job. Include the story, the number and the prompt.

48. Use what you learn from each customer to improve the brain for the next one. That's how the network effect builds.

49. Once the system works, apply it to another niche. Keep the agents and change the context.

Everyone has access to the same models. The context you've collected belongs to you.

Gather as much of that context as you can, as quickly as you can.

Set up these loops so the context keeps feeding into the work.

I'd work through it one step at a time. Have fun with the builds.

I built a Chief of Staff, an Ops team, and a 6 AM inbox brief in one sitting.

Walked through the whole setup on video. He started with a blank Grok Bot account, connected Gmail (multiple addresses), Google Calendar, Drive, and ClickUp with one-click plugins, then created the hierarchy on the spot.

First bot: Chief of Staff. He fed it files about his brand, voice, businesses, and goals so everything went into shared memory. Then he had the Chief of Staff spin up the rest:

Ops Manager
Inbox Manager
Calendar Manager
Marketing Manager
Research Manager
Sales Manager

He grouped them into sections on the left (Executive Team, Ops, Research). Then he made group chats so the Inbox Manager and Calendar Manager could talk to each other and surface what actually needed attention on Monday.

The practical unlock is the routines. He told the Inbox Manager: every weekday at 6 AM, scan the personal inbox, label what’s critical, and give a short brief of what needs a reply. The bot created the scheduled task itself. He can open the routine later, run a test, or turn it off.

Each bot has its own cloud computer with a terminal and file system. The whole setup stays live on the phone and desktop because it lives on the same Grok cloud. He also pulled an “Overheard” bot from the marketplace that watches Reddit, Hacker News, and X for mentions.

The structure is simple on purpose. You mainly talk to the Chief of Staff or the executive group. The specialists stay focused on one job so they don’t burn context. For someone who has never run agents before, this is the fastest path from “I connected my email” to “I have a team that checks the inbox before I wake up.”

How many of your daily checks still start with you opening the apps yourself?
